newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard seeks to mend fences with China.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard seeks to mend fences with China.

text.p: Australia, the outsider of Asia, will attempt to rebuild its relations with the region this week when Prime Minister John Howard visits China and Singapore.

Australia's relations with China have been strained by a series of rows since Howard's Liberal-National coalition took power a year ago, with the country increasingly on the outer with its neighbours over issues ranging from defence to racism.
A senior Australian official told reporters in a pre-trip briefing Howard would seek to improve the troubled relationship with China, boosting trade, economic and political links.

"There's a very strong relationship between Australia and China already and the prime minister would like to see ... his visit as marking a new effort to strengthen it a lot more and to build up the economic relationship a lot more and political co-operation and regional co-operation," the official said.
Both sides acknowledge relations have been hurt by a series of spats, the latest being China's criticism of Australia's growing military and foreign policy ties with the United States.
Over 27,000 military personnel from Australia and the United States this month took part in Tandem Thrust, the biggest joint operation between the two allies since World War Two.

A senior Chinese foreign ministry official said last week that Beijing was "very concerned" and that "we don't think the strengthening of bilateral military ties conforms with the international trend".
Beijing's ire was also raised by ministerial visits to Taiwan and Howard's decision to meet exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama last year.
Australian newspapers have also cited leaked cables from Australian diplomats warning that Beijing would not tolerate a tough stand on human rights by Howard.

Australia's stand over such issues has been weakened by a race debate sparked last year by the maiden parliamentary speech of independent politician Pauline Hanson, who said Asians were swamping Australia.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, who will also meet Howard, said the debate had hurt relations between his country and Australia.
He added that, despite Howard's efforts in the coming weeks, Australia would find it difficult to cement a place in Asia.
"It will always be one foot out," Goh told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio this week.

"It's not quite independent of Asia and it's not, shall we say, in terms of the colour of your skin ... your political thinking (and) your total social environment are different from Asians," Goh said.
China is Australia's fifth largest trading partner, with two-way trade worth A$7.9 billion (US$6.3 billion) in the year to June 30, 1996.

Howard, who will be accompanied by a 20-strong delegation of senior business people, will from Australia to Singapore on Wednesday, before moving on to Shanghai and Beijing, returning to Canberra on April 2.
He will meet leaders in both countries, including Chinese Prime Minister Li Peng and President Jiang Zemin and, in Singapore, Goh and Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew.
